lessons.title: Read a vector

steps.headline: A vector is a list of numbers in a fixed order: how far across, then how far up.

lead.text: The pair (4, 1) means 4 across and 1 up. Each number in it is a coordinate. We call the across number x and the up number y.
The order is part of the meaning. (4, 1) and (1, 4) point to different places.
Coordinates say how far to go across and how far up. A vector is written (x, y).

reveal.text: You reasoned from what the numbers mean. Zero across and zero up is no movement at all, and that vector has a name: the zero vector.

steps.headline: Read the vector (−4, 1): what are x and y?

workedSteps.text: The pair is written (x, y), so x is the first number.
y is the second number. A minus sign means left or down.

steps.headline: Are (1, 4) and (4, 1) the same vector?

workedSteps.text: Write each pair as (x, y).
Compare the x coordinates, then the y coordinates. Are the vectors the same?

lead.text: Read the first number, and keep its sign.

reveal.text: You read x straight from the first position. The −2 is y: it sends the arrow down, not left.

lead.text: A robot's move is written as a vector (across, up). The move (2, 5) means 2 across and 5 up.

lessons.orientation: Read signed coordinates and distinguish vectors from individual scalars.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A café is 4 blocks east and 1 block north of you. A bank is 1 block east and 4 blocks north.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read the across and up numbers of a vector, and say why (1, 4) and (4, 1) are different.

recap.keyIdea: A vector is an ordered list of coordinates: across first, then up. Swap the numbers and you have a different vector.

blocks.text: You read x = 3 from (3, −2), showed that (1, 4) and (4, 1) are different vectors, and found that (0, 0) goes nowhere.

recap.nextHook: Once you can read a vector, you can combine two of them or stretch one.

lessons.title: Add and scale vectors

steps.headline: Add vectors by adding matching coordinates. Scale a vector by multiplying every coordinate by one number.

lead.text: Across adds to across and up adds to up. Subtracting works the same way. A plain number that scales a vector is called a scalar.
Think of each vector as a walk. First walk (2, 1), then walk (−1, 3). Across and up are tracked separately.

reveal.text: You added the across parts and left the up parts alone. That is vector addition: matching coordinates only.

workedSteps.text: Scale first. Multiply both coordinates by 2.
Now add matching coordinates.

steps.headline: Find the y coordinate of 3(2, −1).

workedSteps.text: Multiply every coordinate by 3. The x coordinate first.
Now the y coordinate.

lead.text: A negative scalar stretches the vector and flips it round. Every coordinate still gets multiplied.

reveal.text: You multiplied by a negative number, so the coordinate changed sign as well as size. That is the flip.

lead.text: A drone's flights are vectors (across, up). Two flights in a row add the same way vectors do.

lessons.orientation: Combine displacements, scale every coordinate and handle negative scalars.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: You walk 2 blocks east and 1 block north. Then you walk 1 block west and 3 blocks north.

intro.promise: By the end you'll add vectors, subtract them and scale them, one coordinate at a time.

recap.keyIdea: Vectors add and subtract coordinate by coordinate. A scalar multiplies every coordinate, and a negative scalar also reverses the direction.

blocks.text: You found that (2, 1) + (−1, 3) has x = 1, tripled (2, −1) to get y = −3, and showed that a vector plus its opposite is the zero vector.

recap.nextHook: Next, multiply matching coordinates and add the products: the dot product, which measures length.

lessons.title: Dot products and length

steps.headline: The dot product multiplies matching coordinates and adds the products. The result is one number, not a vector.

lead.text: Write the dot product of two vectors with a dot between them.
Multiply across by across, up by up, then add. You end with a single number.
A vector (x, y) goes x across and y up. Its arrow is the long side of a right-angled triangle with those two short sides.

reveal.text: You used Pythagoras. Squaring each coordinate and adding is the same as a vector's dot product with itself. Its square root is the length.

steps.headline: Find the length of (−7, 24).

workedSteps.text: Square each coordinate and add. This is the vector's dot product with itself.
Add the squares.
The length is the positive square root.
Multiply matching coordinates.
Add the two products. What is the dot product?

lead.text: Dot a vector with itself and every product is a number times itself. Keep the signs as you go.

reveal.text: Each product was a number times itself, so both came out positive. A vector's dot product with itself is never negative.

lead.text: A hiker's displacement is a vector in kilometres, (across, up). Her distance from the start is the length of that vector.

lessons.orientation: Use matching-coordinate products to measure alignment and vector length.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A rectangular field is 9 m wide and 12 m long. You can walk round two sides of it, or straight across.

intro.promise: By the end you'll multiply matching coordinates to get a dot product, and use one to find a vector's length.

recap.keyIdea: The dot product multiplies matching coordinates and adds the products into one number. A vector's dot product with itself is its squared length.

blocks.text: You found (2, 1) · (3, −2) = 4, saw that (3, 4) has length 5, and showed that (−6, 8) is as long as (6, 8) because squaring removes the sign.

recap.nextHook: A dot product of zero means something special about the angle between two vectors.

lessons.title: Orthogonal and unit vectors

steps.headline: Orthogonal vectors have a dot product of zero. A unit vector has length 1.

lead.text: Two vectors are orthogonal when their dot product is zero: they meet at a right angle. A unit vector has length 1. A set of vectors that are orthogonal and all unit is orthonormal.
Vector (1, 2) goes 1 across and 2 up. Vector (−2, 1) goes 2 back and 1 up. Find their dot product.

reveal.text: You found that the two products cancel. A dot product of zero means the vectors are orthogonal: the arrows meet at a right angle.

steps.headline: Make (5, 12) into a unit vector.

workedSteps.text: Find the length.
Divide every coordinate by the length.

steps.headline: Find the x coordinate of the unit vector in the direction (3, 4).

workedSteps.text: Find the length.
Divide the x coordinate by the length. Give it as a decimal.

lead.text: The length of a vector is never negative. Dividing by it keeps the signs of the coordinates.

reveal.text: You divided by a positive length, so the sign of the coordinate was kept. The result is a unit vector that still points the same way.

lead.text: A game turns a velocity into a direction by dividing it by its length. A character is standing still, so its velocity is (0, 0).

lessons.orientation: Recognise perpendicular vectors and turn a nonzero vector into a unit vector.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A step of (6, 8) metres is 10 m long. You want a step in exactly the same direction that is only 1 m long.

intro.promise: By the end you'll test whether two vectors are perpendicular, and shrink any nonzero vector to length 1.

recap.keyIdea: Vectors are orthogonal when their dot product is zero. Dividing a nonzero vector by its length gives a unit vector in the same direction.

blocks.text: You found (1, 2) · (−2, 1) = 0, turned (3, 4) into a unit vector with x = 0.6, and saw that (0, 0) cannot be normalised because its length is zero.

recap.nextHook: Matrices store whole tables of numbers. First you need to read their rows and columns.

lessons.title: Matrix shape and transpose

steps.headline: A matrix is a table of numbers. Its shape is its rows by its columns, and its transpose flips it.

lead.text: Rows run across and columns run down. A matrix with 2 rows and 3 columns has shape 2 × 3. Entry (i, j) sits in row i and column j.
The transpose Aᵀ turns row i into column i. Entry (i, j) of A becomes entry (j, i) of Aᵀ.
A matrix times a vector pairs each entry of a row with an entry of the vector, one by one. A has 2 rows and 3 columns.

reveal.text: You matched the vector to a row of A. Each row is as long as the matrix has columns, so the vector needs exactly that many entries.

steps.headline: Find the transpose of a 2 × 3 matrix with rows (1, 2, 3) and (4, 5, 6).

workedSteps.text: Row 1 becomes column 1, and row 2 becomes column 2.
The shape flips from 2 × 3 to 3 × 2.

steps.headline: Find entry (3, 2) of Aᵀ, where A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&4&-2\\3&0&5\end{pmatrix}$.

workedSteps.text: Transposing swaps the positions. Entry (3, 2) of Aᵀ is entry (2, 3) of A.
Read entry (2, 3) of A. Count rows and columns from 1.

lead.text: The matrix A is $\begin{pmatrix}1&4&-2\\3&0&5\end{pmatrix}$. Transposing turns every row of A into a column.

reveal.text: You counted the rows of A, because those become the columns of Aᵀ. Shape 2 × 3 flips to 3 × 2.

lead.text: A table of sales is the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&4&-2\\3&0&5\end{pmatrix}$. Each row is a shop and each column is a day.

lessons.orientation: Read rows and columns, transpose entries and check input dimensions.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A timetable has 4 days across the top and 7 periods down the side. You flip it so that the days run down the side.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read a matrix's shape and flip it with the transpose, finding any entry by its row and column.

recap.keyIdea: A matrix is a table with a shape of rows by columns. Its transpose swaps the two: entry (i, j) moves to position (j, i).

blocks.text: You saw that a matrix with three columns needs a three-entry vector, found entry (3, 2) of Aᵀ, and showed that transposing swaps the row and column counts.

recap.nextHook: A matrix acting on a vector is a map. Next, see how its columns decide where every vector goes.

lessons.title: Linear transformations

steps.headline: A matrix turns an input vector into an output. A map that respects adding and scaling is called linear.

lead.text: Each entry of A v is one row of A dotted with v. Such a map T is a linear transformation: it keeps sums and scaling.

lead.latex: T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v) \qquad T(cv) = c\,T(v)

lead.text: The first entry of A v is the first row of A dotted with v. Here A is $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and v = (1, 2).

reveal.text: You dotted the first row with v. Each output entry has its own row, and the rows of A decide the output.

steps.headline: Find A(1, 0) for A = $\begin{pmatrix}5&-2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$.

workedSteps.text: Dot each row with (1, 0).
The output is the first column of A.

steps.headline: Find the second coordinate of A(1, 0), for A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\3&1\end{pmatrix}$.

workedSteps.text: The second output entry is the second row of A, (3, 1), dotted with the input (1, 0).
Work it out. What is the second coordinate?

lead.text: Take the first row of A and dot it with the input. Here A is $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\-1&3\end{pmatrix}$ and the input is (2, 1).

reveal.text: You dotted a row with the input. Doing every row gives the whole output, one entry per row.

lead.text: A game shifts every point one unit to the right: S(v) = v + (1, 0). Test any map by asking where it sends the zero vector.

lessons.orientation: Apply a matrix and distinguish linear maps from translations.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A machine takes a point (x, y). It gives back 2x + y across and y up.

intro.promise: By the end you'll apply a matrix to a vector, and test whether a map keeps sums, scaling and the origin.

recap.keyIdea: A matrix maps vectors by dotting each of its rows with the input. Linear maps keep sums and scaling, so zero stays at zero and the columns show where the axes go.

blocks.text: You found that the first output of A v is 4, read a column of a matrix from A(1, 0), and showed that a shift is not linear because zero moves.

recap.nextHook: Two maps in a row make a new map. Next, multiply their matrices to see which order they act in.

lessons.title: Compose matrix maps

steps.headline: A B means do B first, then A. Entry (i, j) of A B is row i of A dotted with column j of B.

lead.text: Applying one map and then another is composing them. The matrix of the composed map is the product A B.
A B v means A(B v). The inner matrix acts first, and the order of the two matrices matters.
The expression A B v is short for A(B v).

reveal.text: You read it from the inside out. In a product of maps, the matrix nearest the vector acts first.

steps.headline: Compare A B v with B A v for A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, B = $\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ and v = (1, 1).

workedSteps.text: B acts first, then A.
Swap the order. A acts first, then B.

steps.headline: Find entry (1, 2) of A B, for A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and B = $\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$.

workedSteps.text: Entry (1, 2) uses row 1 of A, which is (1, 2), and column 2 of B, which is (0, 3).
Dot the row with the column. What is the entry?

lead.text: Let A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and B = $\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$. Entry (2, 1) pairs row 2 of A with column 1 of B.

reveal.text: You paired a row of A with a column of B and added the products. That is the rule for every entry of a product.

lead.text: Matrix A holds the prices of 3 products in 2 shops, so it is 2 × 3. Matrix B holds the sales of those 3 products in 2 months, so it is 3 × 2.

lessons.orientation: Multiply compatible matrices and keep the order of composition.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Machine P doubles a number and machine Q adds 3 to it. You start with 5. In one run you use P and then Q. In another you use Q and then P.

intro.promise: By the end you'll multiply two matrices entry by entry, and say which map acts first in a product.

recap.keyIdea: A matrix product is two maps in a row, and B acts first. Swap the order and the result usually changes. Entry (i, j) is row i of A dotted with column j of B.

blocks.text: You found that entry (1, 2) of A B is 6 while the reversed product gives 4, and that a 2 × 3 matrix times a 3 × 2 matrix gives a 2 × 2 matrix.

recap.nextHook: Some maps can be undone. Next: the identity matrix, and when an inverse exists.

lessons.title: Identity and inverses

steps.headline: The identity matrix changes nothing. The inverse of A undoes A.

lead.text: The identity matrix I has ones on its diagonal and zeros elsewhere. I v = v for every v. The inverse A⁻¹ undoes A, so A⁻¹ A = I and A A⁻¹ = I.
The 2 × 2 identity matrix has ones on its diagonal and zeros elsewhere. It leaves every vector as it was.

reveal.text: You reasoned that undoing a map that does nothing needs no change. The identity is its own inverse.

steps.headline: Find the inverse of A = $\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\5&2\end{pmatrix}$.

workedSteps.text: Find ad − bc, from the entries a = 3, b = 1, c = 5 and d = 2.
Swap the diagonal entries and negate the other two, then divide by ad − bc.
If ad − bc were zero, this division would fail and there would be no inverse.

steps.headline: Find entry (2, 2) of the inverse of A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$.

workedSteps.text: Find ad − bc.
Swap the diagonal entries and negate the other two, then divide by that number. What is entry (2, 2) of the inverse?

lead.text: The matrix A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ has ad − bc equal to 1, so dividing by it changes nothing.

reveal.text: You swapped the diagonal and negated the off-diagonal entry. The inverse of a shear is the shear in the opposite direction.

lead.text: A machine with matrix A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$ turned a hidden input v into the output (1, −2). Undo the machine to recover v.

lessons.orientation: Undo an invertible square map and recognise when an inverse cannot exist.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A machine doubles a number and then adds 3. This time it gave back 17.

intro.promise: By the end you'll undo a matrix map with its inverse, and spot a matrix that has no inverse.

recap.keyIdea: An inverse undoes a map: A⁻¹A is the identity. A 2 × 2 matrix has one when ad − bc is not zero, and then A v = b is solved by v = A⁻¹b.

blocks.text: You found that the identity is its own inverse, inverted [(2, 1); (1, 1)] to get 2 in the corner, and recovered an input by undoing the map.

recap.nextHook: Undoing a map is the same as solving equations. Next: row reduction, which solves them without a formula.

lessons.title: Solve by row reduction

steps.headline: Write a system as an augmented matrix, then simplify it with row operations that keep every solution.

lead.text: An augmented matrix puts the right-hand sides beside the coefficients, one row per equation. A row operation never changes the solution. Swapping two rows is one. Adding a multiple of one row to another is a second, and scaling a row by a nonzero number is the last.
Two equations: x₁ + x₂ = 5 and 2x₁ − x₂ = 1. Adding two true equations gives another true equation.

reveal.text: You added the equations so that x₂ cancelled. Row operations do the same job in an organised way.

steps.headline: Solve x₁ + 2x₂ = 7 and 3x₁ + 5x₂ = 18.

workedSteps.text: Write the augmented matrix.
Subtract 3 × row 1 from row 2. Do it to the right-hand side too.
Row 2 says −x₂ = −3, so x₂ = 3. Put that in row 1: x₁ + 6 = 7.

steps.headline: Start from x₁ + x₂ = 5 and 2x₁ − x₂ = 1. Perform R₂ ← R₂ − 2R₁.

workedSteps.text: Subtract twice row 1 from row 2, entry by entry. The first entry becomes 2 − 2 = 0.
Now the right-hand side. What is the new right side of row 2?

lead.text: After reducing, the second equation is −3x₂ = −9 and the first is x₁ + x₂ = 5. Solve the one with a single unknown.

reveal.text: You solved the simple row first. That is back-substitution: work up from the row with one unknown.

lead.text: Sometimes the first equation has no x₁ in it. Rows can be swapped, so start with whichever equation is simplest.

lessons.orientation: Use equivalent row operations to solve A x = b and check the result.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A pen and a pencil cost £5 together. A pen and two pencils cost £7.

intro.promise: By the end you'll solve a system of equations by row operations, then check your answer.

recap.keyIdea: Row operations keep a system's solution while simplifying it. Reduce until one unknown stands alone, then back-substitute to find the rest.

blocks.text: You found x₁ = 2 by adding equations. You saw that R₂ ← R₂ − 2R₁ leaves −9 on the right, and solved a reduced system.

recap.nextHook: Not every system has exactly one answer. Next: when there are none, or many.

lessons.title: One, none or many solutions

steps.headline: A linear system has one solution, none or infinitely many. The reduced rows tell you which.

lead.text: A row reading 0 = 5, or any nonzero number, is a contradiction: the system has no solution. Otherwise, a column with no pivot is a free variable. It can take any value, so a consistent system with one has infinitely many solutions.
Here the equations name both unknowns outright: x₁ = 2 and x₂ = 3.

reveal.text: You saw that each unknown is fixed by its own equation. Nothing is left free and nothing contradicts, so there is exactly one solution.

steps.headline: Classify x₁ + 2x₂ = 3 and 2x₁ + 4x₂ = 7.

workedSteps.text: Subtract 2 × row 1 from row 2.
The second row says 0 = 1.
No values of x₁ and x₂ can satisfy it. The system has no solution.

steps.headline: Classify x₁ + x₂ = 3 and 2x₁ + 2x₂ = 6.

workedSteps.text: Subtract 2 × row 1 from row 2. The second row becomes all zeros.
The zero row says 0 = 0, which is always true. How many solutions does the system have?

lead.text: The second equation is twice the left side of the first, but its right side is not twice the first's.

reveal.text: You compared the two equations and found them in conflict. After reduction that conflict is a row reading 0 = a nonzero number.

lead.text: A shop's three prices satisfy x₁ + x₃ = 3 and x₂ + 2x₃ = 4. The system is consistent.

lessons.orientation: Classify systems using contradictions, pivots and free variables.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: I'm thinking of two numbers, x and y. I tell you that x + y = 4. I also tell you that 2x + 2y = 9.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell from the reduced rows whether a system has one solution, none or infinitely many.

recap.keyIdea: After row reduction, a row reading 0 = a nonzero number means no solution. A consistent system with a free variable has infinitely many, and with none it has exactly one.

blocks.text: You saw that x₁ = 2 and x₂ = 3 fix one solution, that 0 = 1 rules out any, and that three unknowns with two pivots leave one free variable.

recap.nextHook: The free directions of a system form a shape. Next: spans and subspaces.

lessons.title: Spans and subspaces

steps.headline: A span is every vector you can build from some vectors by scaling and adding. Its dimension counts the independent directions.

lead.text: c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ is a linear combination of v₁ and v₂. All such combinations together form their span. A span may be a line (dimension 1), a plane (dimension 2) or more.
Two vectors give two directions to move in, unless one of them is just a scaled copy of the other.

reveal.text: You checked whether the second vector adds a direction. A scaled copy gives nothing new, so the span stays a line.

workedSteps.text: Match the second coordinates. Only (1, 1) has an up part.
Match the first coordinates: c₁ + c₂ = 7.

steps.headline: Write (5, 3) as c₁(1, 0) + c₂(1, 1). Find c₁.

workedSteps.text: Match the second coordinates.
Match the first coordinates: c₁ + 3 = 5. What is c₁?

lead.text: Compare the two vectors. Is one a multiple of the other, positive or negative?

reveal.text: You found the second vector is a negative multiple of the first. It points back along the same line, so the span is still one line.

steps.headline: A subspace contains the zero vector and stays inside itself when you add members or scale them.

lead.text: A subspace is a set of vectors with two properties. It contains the zero vector. Adding two members, or scaling one, gives another member. Every span is a subspace.
A drone must stay on the path y = 2x + 1. Any subspace has to contain the zero vector, so test the path with that.

lessons.orientation: Describe all linear combinations and test the conditions for a subspace.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A robot can only move in the direction (1, 2), any number of times, forwards or backwards.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the dimension of a span and test whether a set is a subspace.

recap.keyIdea: A span is every combination of some vectors, and its dimension counts the independent directions. A subspace contains zero and stays inside itself under adding and scaling.

blocks.text: You found that (1, 2) and (2, 4) span only a line, wrote (5, 3) with c₁ = 2, and ruled out y = 2x + 1 because it misses the origin.

recap.nextHook: Which vectors do you really need to span a space? Next: bases.

lessons.title: Basis and dimension

steps.headline: A basis spans a space and has no redundancy. Every basis of a space has the same number of vectors: its dimension.

lead.text: Vectors are linearly independent when none of them is a combination of the others. A basis is a set of independent vectors that spans the space. The number of vectors in any basis is the dimension of the space.
A plane is a two-dimensional space. A basis has exactly as many vectors as the space has dimensions.

reveal.text: You matched the size of a basis to the dimension of the space. Any basis of the plane has the same size.

workedSteps.text: Match coordinates. This gives two equations.
Add the equations. The c₂ terms cancel.
Put c₁ back into the first equation.

steps.headline: Write (4, 2) as c₁(1, 1) + c₂(1, −1). Find c₁.

workedSteps.text: Match coordinates.
Add the two equations. What is c₁?

lead.text: Match the second coordinates first, then the first coordinates. Here the basis is (1, 1) and (2, 0).

reveal.text: You found the up coordinate first, then used it for the across coordinate. A basis gave a single answer for each coefficient.

lead.text: A navigation app wants the fewest direction vectors that still reach everywhere. One candidate pair includes the zero vector.

lessons.orientation: Find a spanning independent set and use its vectors as coordinates.

recap.keyIdea: A basis spans a space with no redundancy, and every basis of it has the same size: its dimension. Each vector then has exactly one set of coordinates.

blocks.text: You found that a basis for the plane has two vectors. In the basis (1, 1), (1, −1) you wrote (4, 2) with c₁ = 3.

recap.nextHook: Every matrix has a basis for its outputs and its collapsed inputs. Next: rank and the null space.

lessons.title: Rank and null space

steps.headline: The rank counts a matrix's independent outputs. The null space holds the inputs it sends to zero.

lead.text: The column space is every output A v. Its dimension is the rank, which is the number of pivots. The null space is every input with A v = 0, and its dimension is the nullity.
The null space holds the inputs that A sends to zero. Here A is $\begin{pmatrix}1&2&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$. Dot each row with the input to test one.

reveal.text: You dotted the first row with the input, and it vanished. That input is in the null space, since the second row vanishes too.

steps.headline: Find the rank and nullity of $\begin{pmatrix}1&3&0&2\\0&0&1&4\end{pmatrix}$.

workedSteps.text: The matrix is already reduced. There are pivots in columns 1 and 3.
The matrix has 4 columns. The nullity is the columns that are left over.

steps.headline: Find the rank of A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&2&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$.

workedSteps.text: Row 1 has its first nonzero entry in column 1. Row 2 has its first nonzero entry in column 3.
Count the pivots. What is the rank?

lead.text: The matrix A is $\begin{pmatrix}1&2&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$. It has three columns, and you know its rank.

reveal.text: You took the rank away from the number of columns. Each column without a pivot is a free direction, and those directions are the null space.

lead.text: The column space is built from columns of the original matrix. The pivot columns show which of them are independent.

lessons.orientation: Connect pivot columns, column space and the inputs a matrix sends to zero.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A machine takes a point (x, y) and gives back the number x + y. The point (2, −2) goes to 0.

intro.promise: By the end you'll count a matrix's rank and nullity, and say which inputs it sends to zero.

recap.keyIdea: The rank counts the independent output directions and the nullity counts the inputs sent to zero. Together they add up to the number of columns.

blocks.text: You found rank 2 and nullity 1 for the same three-column matrix, checked that (−2, 1, 0) is sent to zero, and chose columns 1 and 3 as a basis.

recap.nextHook: Maps also stretch area. Next: the determinant, and why zero means a collapse.

lessons.title: Determinants and volume

steps.headline: A 2 × 2 matrix scales area by its determinant, ad − bc. A negative sign records a flip, and zero means a collapse.

lead.text: For the matrix with rows (a, b) and (c, d), the determinant is ad − bc. Its size is the factor by which area changes. Its sign says whether the map flips orientation.
The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}-2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ stretches across by 2 and flips direction, and stretches up by 3. A square of area 1 becomes a rectangle.

reveal.text: You multiplied the two stretches, and ignored the flip when finding area. That product, with its sign, is the determinant.

steps.headline: Find the determinant of $\begin{pmatrix}1&5\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$.

workedSteps.text: Multiply the main diagonal.
Multiply the other diagonal.
Subtract. The area scales by 7, and the sign says orientation flips.

steps.headline: Find the determinant of $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$.

workedSteps.text: Main diagonal product.
Other diagonal product.
Subtract the second from the first. What is the determinant?

lead.text: Swapping two rows of a matrix changes its determinant. Here the rows of the previous matrix are swapped: $\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$.

reveal.text: You found the same size with the opposite sign. Swapping rows flips orientation, and the sign records it.

lead.text: A diagonal map scales each direction on its own. The volume factor is the product of the three scales. A cube of volume 1 m³ becomes a box.

lessons.orientation: Read signed area and volume factors and use zero determinant to detect collapse.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A map stretches every length across by 5 and every length up by 2. It turns a square of side 1 m into a rectangle.

intro.promise: By the end you'll calculate a 2 × 2 determinant and read what it says about area.

recap.keyIdea: A determinant is the signed factor by which a map scales area or volume. Zero means the map collapses space, so there is no inverse.

blocks.text: You found det = 5, then −5 after swapping its rows. Dependent columns gave 0, and scale factors multiplied to 24 and 12.

recap.nextHook: Closest-point problems come next: projecting a vector onto a direction.

lessons.title: Project onto a direction

steps.headline: The projection of v onto d is the point on d's line that is closest to v. What is left over is the residual.

lead.text: Scale d by the coefficient (v · d) ÷ (d · d) to land on the projection. The residual is v minus the projection, and it makes a right angle with d.
The direction (2, 0) points along the x axis. Projecting a point drops it straight onto that line.

reveal.text: You kept the across position and dropped the height. Projecting onto the x axis does exactly that.

steps.headline: Project v = (5, 1) onto d = (1, 1), then find the residual.

workedSteps.text: Dot v with d, and d with itself.
The coefficient is 6 ÷ 2. Scale d by it.
Subtract the projection from v to get the residual.

steps.headline: Project (4, 2) onto the line spanned by (1, 1). Find the x coordinate.

workedSteps.text: Dot the vectors.
Scale d by the coefficient. What is the x coordinate of the projection?

lead.text: The vector is (−2, 4) and the direction is (1, 1). Follow the same steps as before.

reveal.text: Your answer is a multiple of (1, 1). A projection always lies on the line it projects onto.

lead.text: A kite is pulled with force (4, 2). Along the rope's direction (1, 1) the pull is (3, 3). The sideways part is the residual: the force minus that pull.

lessons.orientation: Find the closest vector on a line and a perpendicular residual.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A point sits at (6, 5): 6 along the ground and 5 up. It is dropped straight down onto the horizontal ground line.

intro.promise: By the end you'll project a vector onto a direction, and find the perpendicular part that is left over.

recap.keyIdea: The projection of v onto d is ((v · d) ÷ (d · d)) d, the closest point on the line. The residual v − projection is perpendicular to d.

blocks.text: You found the projection of (4, 2) onto (1, 1) has x = 3, saw that the residual is (1, −1), and showed that a perpendicular vector projects to zero.

recap.nextHook: When no exact answer exists, the closest one is a projection too. Next: least squares.

lessons.title: Fit with least squares

steps.headline: Least squares picks the fit whose squared residuals add up to the smallest total.

lead.text: A residual is a measurement minus the fitted value. When no fit matches every measurement, add up the squares of all the residuals. The least-squares fit makes that total smallest.
A single constant cannot equal 2, 4 and 9 at once. Choose the one that treats the three measurements fairly.

reveal.text: You balanced the three measurements. For a single constant, the least-squares fit is exactly their mean.

steps.headline: Fit one constant to 2, 3 and 10, then total the squared residuals.

workedSteps.text: The best constant is the mean: 15 ÷ 3.
The residuals are measurement minus fit. They add up to zero.
Square each residual and add.

steps.headline: Measurements 2, 4 and 9 are fitted by the constant 5. Total the squared residuals.

workedSteps.text: The residuals are 2 − 5, 4 − 5 and 9 − 5.
Square each one and add. What is the total?

lead.text: The residuals of the fit 5 to the measurements 2, 4 and 9 are −3, −1 and 4. Add them as they are, with their signs.

reveal.text: You found they cancel. Residuals of a least-squares constant always sum to zero, so errors above and below balance.

lead.text: A taxi's fare is £2, £5 and £8 for trips of 0, 1 and 2 km. A line c + sx has slope s. For points at x = 0, 1, 2, the best-fit slope is (last y − first y) ÷ 2.

lessons.orientation: Fit inconsistent measurements by minimising squared residuals.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: You measure the same length three times and get 6 cm, 7 cm and 11 cm. You want one fair value to report.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the best constant or line for measurements that disagree, by making the squared errors smallest.

recap.keyIdea: When measurements cannot all be matched, least squares picks the fit with the smallest sum of squared residuals. For a constant, that fit is the mean.

blocks.text: You found that 5 is the best constant for 2, 4 and 9. Its squared residuals total 26.

recap.nextHook: Next, build perpendicular unit vectors step by step: the orthonormal basis.

lessons.title: Build an orthonormal basis

steps.headline: Gram–Schmidt makes perpendicular unit vectors: normalise the first, remove it from the next, then normalise what is left.

lead.text: Start with independent vectors. Divide the first by its length. From the second, subtract its projection onto the first. The residual is perpendicular to the first, so divide it by its length too.
Removing the part of v that lies along a direction leaves the part that does not. The direction here is the x axis, (1, 0), and v = (3, 1).

reveal.text: You removed the part along the x axis. What is left points straight up, perpendicular to the direction you removed.

steps.headline: Make an orthonormal pair from (3, 4) and (1, 0).

workedSteps.text: Divide the first vector by its length, 5.
Subtract the projection of (1, 0) onto e₁. The dot product is 0.6.
The residual has length 0.8. Divide by it to get a unit vector.

steps.headline: Normalise (1, 1). Find its first coordinate as a decimal.

workedSteps.text: Find the length.
Divide the first coordinate by √2. What is it as a decimal?

lead.text: The vector is (−3, 4). Find its length, then divide the coordinate the question asks for.

reveal.text: You divided by the length, and the result has length 1. Normalising keeps the direction and fixes the size.

lead.text: Take u = (1, 1) and v = (2, 2). Remove from v its projection onto u, then ask whether a second perpendicular direction is left.

lessons.orientation: Subtract projections and normalise the remaining independent directions.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A vector points to (4, 7): 4 across and 7 up. You cut off the part of it that lies along the x axis.

intro.promise: By the end you'll turn two independent vectors into two perpendicular unit vectors, step by step.

recap.keyIdea: Gram–Schmidt builds an orthonormal basis: normalise the first vector, subtract each earlier direction from the next, then normalise what is left.

blocks.text: You removed the part of (1, 0) along (1, 1). You normalised (1, 1) and (−3, 4).

recap.nextHook: Some directions are special for a map: it only stretches them. Next: eigenvectors.

lessons.title: Eigenvectors and eigenvalues

steps.headline: An eigenvector is a nonzero vector that a matrix only scales. The scale factor is its eigenvalue.

lead.text: Most vectors turn when a matrix acts on them. An eigenvector v does not: its output stays on the same line, so A v = λv. The number λ is the eigenvalue.
Let A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ and v = (1, 1). Work out A v by dotting each row with v, then compare the output with v.

reveal.text: You found the output is a multiple of the input. That is what makes (1, 1) an eigenvector of this matrix.

steps.headline: Show that (1, 1) is an eigenvector of $\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$, and find λ.

workedSteps.text: Work out A v.
Compare with v. The output is a multiple of the input.

steps.headline: Find λ for A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ and v = (1, −1).

workedSteps.text: Work out A v.
A v is λ times v. What is λ?

lead.text: The matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}-2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ and v = (1, 0). Work out A v and compare it with v.

reveal.text: You found the output points opposite to the input. A negative eigenvalue flips the direction along that line.

lead.text: Test a candidate by working out A v. If the output is not on the same line as v, the candidate is not an eigenvector.

lessons.orientation: Find nonzero directions that a square map changes only by a scalar.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A machine turns the vector (1, 2) into the vector (4, 8).

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the scale factor a matrix applies along a special direction, and test whether a vector is such a direction.

recap.keyIdea: An eigenvector is a nonzero vector that a matrix only scales: A v = λv. The scale factor λ is its eigenvalue, and it may be negative or zero.

blocks.text: You found λ = 3 along (1, 1) and λ = 1 along (1, −1) for one matrix. You also saw that (1, 0) is not an eigenvector.

recap.nextHook: With enough eigenvectors, a matrix becomes simple stretches. Next: diagonalisation.

lessons.title: Diagonalise a map

steps.headline: With enough independent eigenvectors, A = P D P⁻¹. P holds the eigenvectors and D holds the eigenvalues.

lead.text: Put independent eigenvectors in the columns of P. Put their eigenvalues on the diagonal of D, in the same order. Then A = P D P⁻¹, which is called diagonalising A. Along each eigenvector, A just scales.
A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$. Each diagonal entry of D is the eigenvalue of the matching column of P.

reveal.text: You found the eigenvalue of the first column of P. That number sits in the first diagonal slot of D.

steps.headline: Apply $\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$ twice to its eigenvector (1, 1), which has eigenvalue 5.

workedSteps.text: One application multiplies by 5.
The second application multiplies by 5 again.

steps.headline: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ and v = (1, 1), find the scalar that multiplies v in A²v.

workedSteps.text: This eigenvector has eigenvalue 3, so A v = 3v.
Apply A again. What scalar multiplies v in A²v?

lead.text: A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ and v = (1, 0), which has eigenvalue 2. Each application of A multiplies v by that eigenvalue.

reveal.text: You multiplied by the eigenvalue once per application. After n applications the scalar is λ to the power n.

lead.text: Reorder the columns of P and the entries of D must reorder with them. Each eigenvalue stays beside its own eigenvector. Now (1, −1) is the first column of P.

lessons.orientation: Use an eigenvector basis to separate a square map into independent scalings.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A machine triples every vector along (1, 1) and leaves every vector along (1, −1) unchanged. The vector (2, 0) is (1, 1) + (1, −1).

intro.promise: By the end you'll write a matrix as P D P⁻¹ and use D to apply that matrix again and again.

recap.keyIdea: A matrix with a basis of eigenvectors is P D P⁻¹. P's columns are the eigenvectors and D holds their eigenvalues in the same order, so powers act as λⁿ.

blocks.text: You read 3 and 1 off D for two eigenvectors of one matrix. You found that applying A twice multiplies (1, 1) by 9.

recap.nextHook: Every matrix, even a rectangular one, has a similar split. Next: the singular value decomposition.

lessons.title: Singular value decomposition

steps.headline: Every matrix splits as A = U Σ Vᵀ: one stretch between two length-preserving turns.

lead.text: U and V are orthogonal, so they only rotate or reflect. Σ is diagonal and holds the stretch sizes, called singular values. They are never negative, and the number of positive ones equals the rank.
A = $\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&-2\end{pmatrix}$ stretches across by 3 and up by 2, and flips up. Singular values record only the sizes of the stretches.

reveal.text: You compared the sizes of the stretches and ignored the flip. Singular values measure size only.

steps.headline: Find the singular values of $\begin{pmatrix}-6&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$.

workedSteps.text: The two columns are perpendicular. Their lengths are the stretch sizes.
The minus sign is a flip, so it goes into U. Σ keeps only the sizes.

steps.headline: Find the smaller singular value of $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$.

workedSteps.text: The second row is twice the first, so the rank is 1.
The number of positive singular values equals the rank. What is the smaller singular value?

lead.text: The matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&2&0\end{pmatrix}$. It has two nonzero stretches, one per row.

reveal.text: You read the stretches off the matrix and took the smaller. Singular values are usually listed from the largest to the smallest.

lead.text: A 2 × 3 matrix takes three inputs to two outputs. In the full SVD, Σ has the same shape as A, with the singular values along its diagonal.

lessons.orientation: Separate a rectangular map into orthogonal coordinate changes and nonnegative stretches.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A machine stretches every vector across by 4 and up by 2, then spins the whole plane a quarter turn.

intro.promise: By the end you'll split any matrix into two length-preserving turns and one stretch, and read its singular values.

recap.keyIdea: Every matrix is A = U Σ Vᵀ. U and Vᵀ preserve length, and Σ holds the nonnegative singular values: the stretches. The number of positive ones is the rank.

blocks.text: You read the largest singular value of diag(3, −2) as 3, found that a rank-one matrix has a singular value of 0, and matched the shape of Σ to A.

hints: Which of the two numbers comes first?
x is the across coordinate, and the pair is written (x, y).
Read the first number, keeping its sign.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first coordinate is 3; the second is −2.

questions.onCorrect: x is the first number. The −2 belongs to y and sends the vector downwards.

hints: Compare the first numbers, then the second numbers.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. The x coordinates differ, so the vectors differ.

questions.onCorrect: No. Same numbers in a different order give a different vector.

questions.prompt: How far from where it starts does the zero vector (0, 0) take you?
hints: What do the two numbers say about moving across and up?
A coordinate of nothing means no movement in that direction.
No movement across and no movement up. Where do you end up?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: No movement across and none up, so you stay at the start: 0 units away.

questions.onCorrect: No movement across and none up: the zero vector leaves you exactly where you started.

misconceptions.feedback: That would be one step of movement. Both coordinates say there is none.

questions.prompt: How many units up does the robot's move (0, 1) take it?
hints: Which position in the pair says how far up?
The pair is (across, up).
Read the second number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The second coordinate is the up distance, and it is 1.

questions.onCorrect: The second number is the up distance. This move goes straight up and not at all across.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the across number. The up number is the second one.

questions.prompt: Give the x coordinate of (−5, 3).
hints: Which position names x?
Coordinates are ordered (x, y). Keep the sign you read.
Report the first entry, including its minus sign.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first coordinate is −5.

questions.onCorrect: −5. The sign is part of the coordinate: it means 5 units the other way across.

misconceptions.feedback: That is y, the second coordinate. x is the first number, with its sign.
Check the sign. A minus sign is part of the coordinate.

questions.prompt: Give the y coordinate of (6, −4).
hints: Which position names y?
Coordinates are ordered (x, y).
Report the second entry, keeping its sign.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The second coordinate is −4.

questions.onCorrect: −4. y is the second number, and its minus sign says the vector goes down.

misconceptions.feedback: That is x, the first coordinate. y is the second number.
The sign is missing. Read the minus sign along with the number.

questions.prompt: What is the x coordinate of (2, 1) + (−1, 3)?
hints: Which coordinate does the question ask for?
Combine only the across entries, with their signs.
Add the first entry of each vector.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The x coordinate is 2 + (−1) = 1.

questions.onCorrect: Add the across entries, signs included: 2 + (−1). The up entries do not mix in.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts the second entry from the first. The sum adds the two across entries as written.
That multiplies the two across entries. Add them.

questions.prompt: What is the y coordinate of 3(2, −1)?
hints: Which entry is the y coordinate?
Multiply it by the scalar, keeping its sign.
A positive scalar times a negative number gives a negative number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The y coordinate is 3 × (−1) = −3.

questions.onCorrect: Multiply every coordinate by the scalar: 3 × (−1) = −3.

misconceptions.feedback: That scales the x coordinate. The question asks for y.
That is y before scaling. Multiply it by the scalar.

questions.prompt: What is the x coordinate of −2(2, −1)?
hints: Apply the scalar to the first coordinate.
A negative scalar flips the sign of what it multiplies.
Multiply the first entry by the negative scalar.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first coordinate becomes −2 × 2 = −4.

questions.onCorrect: A negative scalar flips the sign and stretches: −2 × 2 = −4.

misconceptions.feedback: The sign is missing. A negative scalar times a positive entry is negative.
That adds the scalar to the entry. A scalar multiplies.

questions.prompt: A drone flies (3, 2) and then flies (−3, −2). How far up is it from its start?
hints: Add the up parts of the two flights.
One flight went up and the other came back down.
Add the second entries, with their signs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The vertical movements add to 2 − 2 = 0.

questions.onCorrect: The second flight undoes the first: a vector plus its negative is the zero vector.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the sizes and ignores the sign. The second flight goes the other way.

questions.prompt: Let u = (2, 1) and v = (−1, 3). What is the y coordinate of 2u + v?
hints: Scale u before adding v.
Double each entry of u, then add the matching entries of v.
Double the second entry of u, then add the second entry of v.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: First 2u = (4, 2); adding v gives (3, 5), so y = 5.

questions.onCorrect: Double u to get (4, 2). Adding v entry by entry gives (3, 5), so y is 5.

misconceptions.feedback: That is u + v, where u was not doubled first.

questions.prompt: What is the x coordinate of (4, 1) − (1, 3)?
hints: Subtracting works entry by entry, like adding.
Take the second vector's across entry away from the first's.
Subtract the first entries.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Subtract matching entries: the first is 4 − 1 = 3.

questions.onCorrect: Subtract entry by entry, first vector first: 4 − 1.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the entries. The question subtracts.
That subtracts in the wrong order. The first vector comes first.

hints: Multiply matching coordinates, then add.
The first product is positive and the second is negative.
Add the two products, keeping the sign of each.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The dot product is 2 × 3 + 1 × (−2) = 6 − 2 = 4.

questions.onCorrect: 6 + (−2) = 4. The result is one number: both signed products added.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the sign of the second product: one of its two entries is negative.

questions.prompt: A vector goes 3 across and 4 up. What is its length?
hints: Picture the right-angled triangle the vector makes.
Square each coordinate, add the squares, then take the square root.
Which whole number multiplied by itself gives the sum of the squares?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The squared length is 9 + 16 = 25, so the length is 5.

questions.onCorrect: Square, add, then take the square root: √(9 + 16) = 5.

A negative times a negative is positive.
The two products are both positive. Add them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The products are 1 and 4, which sum to 5.

hints: Distance is the length of the vector.
Square each coordinate and add. The minus sign disappears.
Take the positive square root of the sum.

hints: Multiply matching coordinates.
The second product has a negative entry in it.
Add the two signed products.

hints: Square both coordinates.
Add the two squares.
Take the positive square root of the sum.

That adds the coordinates. Square them first.

One product is negative.

questions.prompt: A unit vector in the direction (3, 4) has what x coordinate?

Divide the x coordinate by the length.
Write the fraction as a decimal.

hints: Check the dot product, then check both lengths.

The second product is negative.

Find the rank first, then take it away from the number of columns.
The matrix has three columns.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The second row is redundant; rank is one and there are three columns, so nullity is two.

questions.onCorrect: The second row repeats the first, so the rank is one. Three columns less one is two.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the rank. Nullity is the number of columns minus the rank.
That counts all the columns. Take the rank away.

questions.prompt: What is the determinant of $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$?
hints: Multiply the main diagonal, then the other diagonal.
Subtract the second product from the first.
The determinant is ad − bc.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The determinant is 2 × 3 − 1 × 1 = 5.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two products. The determinant subtracts the second from the first.
Check the order: subtract bc from ad.

questions.prompt: What is the determinant of $\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$?
hints: Multiply the main diagonal, then the other diagonal.
The second product is the larger one.
Subtract the second product from the first.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The determinant is 1 × 1 − 3 × 2 = −5.

questions.onCorrect: ad − bc = 1 − 6 = −5. Swapping the rows flipped the sign.

misconceptions.feedback: The sign is missing. The second product is larger, so the result is negative.
That adds the two products. The determinant subtracts the second from the first.

questions.prompt: What is the determinant of $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$?
hints: Multiply the main diagonal, then the other diagonal.
Compare the two products.
Subtract the second from the first.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The diagonal products are both 4, so their difference is zero.

questions.onCorrect: The columns are dependent, so the map flattens the plane and the determinant is zero.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two products. The determinant subtracts the second from the first.

questions.prompt: A map scales lengths by 2 across, 3 up and 4 deep. A cube of volume 1 m³ becomes a box. What is its volume, in cubic metres?
hints: Each direction is scaled on its own.
Volume is across times up times deep.
Multiply the three scales.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Multiply the diagonal scales: 2 × 3 × 4 = 24.

questions.onCorrect: Volume factors multiply: 2 × 3 × 4 = 24.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the scales. Volume multiplies them.

questions.prompt: A = $\begin{pmatrix}-2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$. By what positive factor does A change area?
hints: Each direction is stretched on its own.
The flip does not change how big the area is.
Multiply the sizes of the two stretches.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The determinant is −6. Its absolute value is the area factor 6.

questions.onCorrect: The determinant is −6. Its size, 6, is the area factor.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the determinant. Area itself never goes negative, so use its size.

questions.prompt: A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ and B = $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$. What is det(A B)?
hints: Find det(A) and det(B).
Determinants multiply when matrices multiply.
Multiply the two determinants.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The determinants are 6 and 2; det(A B) = 6 × 2 = 12.

questions.onCorrect: Doing one map after another multiplies the area factors: 6 × 2 = 12.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two determinants. The determinant of a product is their product.

questions.prompt: Project (4, 2) onto the line spanned by (1, 1). What is the x coordinate?
hints: Work out v · d and d · d.
Divide the first by the second to get the coefficient.
Multiply d by the coefficient and read the first entry.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The coefficient is (4 + 2)/(1 + 1) = 3, so the projection is (3, 3).

questions.onCorrect: The coefficient is 6 ÷ 2. Scale d by it to land on the line.

misconceptions.feedback: That is v · d. Divide it by d · d, then scale d.
That is the x coordinate of v itself. Project first.

questions.prompt: Project (3, 4) onto the line spanned by (2, 0). What is the x coordinate?
hints: Which line is spanned by (2, 0)?
Projecting onto the x axis keeps the across position.
Read the across coordinate of the vector.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The line is the x axis, so the projection keeps x = 3 and sets y = 0.

questions.onCorrect: The line is the x axis. Projecting keeps x and drops the height.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the y coordinate of v. The x axis keeps x and drops y.
That is v · d. Divide it by d · d first.

questions.prompt: A force (4, 2) has a pull of (3, 3) along the rope. What is the y coordinate of the sideways part?
hints: The sideways part is the force minus the pull along the rope.
Subtract matching coordinates.
Subtract the pull's y coordinate from the force's y coordinate, in that order.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The residual is v − projection = (1, −1).

questions.onCorrect: Subtract the projection from the force. What remains is perpendicular to the rope.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the y coordinate of the pull along the rope. The sideways part is what is left.

questions.prompt: Project (2, −2) onto the line spanned by (1, 1). What is the x coordinate?
hints: Work out v · d first.
What happens to a coefficient whose top is zero?
Zero times a direction is the zero vector.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Their dot product is zero, so the projection coefficient is zero.

questions.onCorrect: A vector perpendicular to the line has zero projection onto it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the x coordinate of v itself. Dot v with d first.

questions.prompt: Project (2, 5) onto the line spanned by (0, 1). What is the y coordinate?
hints: Which line is spanned by (0, 1)?
Projecting onto the y axis keeps the height.
Read the up coordinate of the vector.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The line is the y axis, so the projection is (0, 5).

questions.onCorrect: The line is the y axis. Projecting keeps y and drops x.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the x coordinate of v. The y axis keeps y and drops x.

questions.prompt: Project (−2, 4) onto the line spanned by (1, 1). What is the x coordinate?
hints: Work out v · d and d · d.
Divide the first by the second.
Multiply d by the coefficient and read the first entry.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The coefficient is (−2 + 4)/2 = 1, giving projection (1, 1).

questions.onCorrect: v · d = 2 and d · d = 2, so the coefficient is 1 and the projection is d itself.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the x coordinate of v itself. Project first.
That is v · d. Divide it by d · d, then scale d.

questions.prompt: Fit one constant to the measurements 2, 4 and 9 by least squares. What constant gives the smallest squared error?
hints: The measurements cannot all be matched. Balance them.
Use all three measurements.
Add them and divide by how many there are.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The mean is (2 + 4 + 9)/3 = 5.

questions.onCorrect: For one constant, least squares gives the mean of the measurements.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the middle measurement. Use all three.
That is the total. Divide it by the number of measurements.

questions.prompt: Measurements 2, 4 and 9 are fitted by the constant 5. What is the sum of the residuals, measurement minus fit?
hints: Find each residual with its sign.
One of them is positive and two are negative.
Add the three residuals.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The residuals are −3, −1 and 4, whose sum is zero.

questions.onCorrect: The misses below and above cancel exactly, because the fit is the mean.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the sizes and ignores the signs. Residuals can be negative.

questions.prompt: Fit y ≈ c + sx to the points (0, 1), (1, 2) and (2, 2) by least squares. What is s?
hints: The points are at equal steps across.
Use the slope shortcut: last y minus first y, over the number of steps.
Subtract the first y from the last y, then halve it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The normal equations are 3c + 3s = 5 and 3c + 5s = 6. Subtracting gives 2s = 1, so s = 0.5.

questions.onCorrect: (2 − 1) ÷ 2 = 0.5. The line cannot hit every point, so this slope balances the misses.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the last y minus the first. Divide by the number of steps across.

questions.prompt: Measurements 2, 4 and 9 are fitted by the constant 5. What is the sum of the squared residuals?
hints: Find each residual: measurement minus fit.
Square each residual.
Add the three squares.
questions.onCorrect: Squares make every miss positive: 9 + 1 + 16 = 26.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the plain sum of the residuals. Square each one first.

questions.prompt: Fit one constant by least squares to the measurements 1, 5 and 9. What is it?
hints: For one constant, the best fit is the mean.
Add the three measurements.
Divide the total by how many there are.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Their mean is 15/3 = 5.

questions.onCorrect: The mean of the measurements is the least-squares constant.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total. Divide it by the number of measurements.

questions.prompt: The fare points (0, 2), (1, 5) and (2, 8) are fitted by y = c + sx. What is s?
hints: How much does y rise for each step in x?
Use the slope shortcut for points at 0, 1 and 2.
Subtract the first y from the last, then divide by the number of steps.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The points lie exactly on y = 2 + 3x, so the least-squares slope is 3.

questions.onCorrect: The points lie exactly on a line, so that line is the best fit.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total rise. Divide it by the number of steps across.

questions.prompt: Subtract the projection of v = (1, 0) onto u = (1, 1). What is the y coordinate of the residual?
hints: Find the projection first.
The projection is the coefficient times u.
Subtract the projection's y from v's y.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The projection is (0.5, 0.5), so the residual is (0.5, −0.5).

questions.onCorrect: The residual is v minus the projection, and it is perpendicular to u.

misconceptions.feedback: The sign is missing. Subtract the projection's y from v's y, in that order.

questions.prompt: Normalise (1, 1). What is its first coordinate as a decimal?
hints: Find the length first.
Divide the first coordinate by that length.
Write the result as a decimal.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The length is √2, so the first unit coordinate is 1/√2 ≈ 0.707107.

questions.onCorrect: The length is √2. Dividing 1 by √2 gives about 0.707107.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the coordinate before dividing by the length.
That multiplies by the length. Divide by it.

questions.prompt: Find (1, 1) · (1, −1), the dot product of the two directions.
hints: Multiply matching coordinates.
One product is negative.
Add the products.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The products 1 and −1 cancel. Normalising both nonzero directions keeps their dot product zero.

questions.onCorrect: The products cancel, so the directions are perpendicular. Normalising keeps that.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the sizes of the products. The second one is negative.

questions.prompt: For u = (1, 1) and v = (2, 2), can the residual of v create a second unit basis vector?
hints: Subtract the projection of v onto u. What is left?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. v lies along u, so its residual is the zero vector, which cannot be normalised.

questions.onCorrect: v lies along u, so the residual is zero. A zero vector cannot be normalised.

misconceptions.feedback: v is a multiple of u. Subtract its projection and nothing is left to normalise.

questions.prompt: Subtract the projection of (3, 1) onto (1, 0). What is the y coordinate of the residual?
hints: The projection onto the x axis keeps the across part.
Subtract it from the vector.
Only the up part is left.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The projection is (3, 0), leaving residual (0, 1).

questions.onCorrect: Remove the part along (1, 0) and only the up part remains.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the x coordinate of the residual. The question asks for y.
That is the x coordinate of v itself. Subtract the projection first.

questions.prompt: Normalise (−3, 4). What is the second coordinate?
hints: Find the length first.
Square both coordinates, add, then take the square root.
Divide the second coordinate by the length.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The length is 5, giving second coordinate 4/5 = 0.8.

questions.onCorrect: The length is 5, and 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the coordinate before dividing by the length.
That is the first coordinate. The question asks for the second.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ and v = (1, 1), find λ in A v = λv.
hints: Work out A v first.
Dot each row of A with v.
Compare A v with v. What is the multiplier?
questions.onCorrect: A v = (3, 3) is 3 times v, so the eigenvalue is 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a coordinate of v. Work out A v first, then compare.
That adds the two entries of A v. Compare A v with v instead.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ and v = (1, −1), find λ in A v = λv.
hints: Work out A v first.
Dot each row of A with v, keeping the signs.
Compare A v with v.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A v = (1, −1), so this direction has eigenvalue 1.

questions.onCorrect: A v equals v, so this direction is left unchanged: eigenvalue 1.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the second coordinate of v. The multiplier is the ratio of output to input.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}-2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ and v = (1, 0), find λ.
hints: Work out A v first.
Dot each row of A with v.
Compare A v with v. Check the sign.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The output is (−2, 0) = −2v.

questions.onCorrect: The output is −2 times v: the eigenvalue is negative, so the direction flips.

misconceptions.feedback: The sign is missing. The output points opposite to the input.
That is the other diagonal entry, which acts on the y direction.

questions.prompt: Is (1, 0) an eigenvector of A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$?
hints: Work out A v. Is it on the same line as v?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. A(1, 0) = (2, 1), which is not a multiple of (1, 0).

questions.onCorrect: A v = (2, 1) is not a multiple of (1, 0), so (1, 0) is not an eigenvector.

misconceptions.feedback: A v comes out as (2, 1), which has an up part that v lacks. It is not a multiple of v.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}4&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$ and v = (0, 1), find λ.
hints: Work out A v first.
Dot each row of A with v.
Compare A v with v.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The output is (0, 2) = 2v.

questions.onCorrect: The output is 2 times v. A diagonal matrix scales each axis by its own entry.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the other diagonal entry, which acts on the x direction.

questions.prompt: A nonzero vector v satisfies A v = 0. Is v an eigenvector?
hints: Write A v = 0 in the form λv.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes. A v = 0 = 0v, so v is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 0.

questions.onCorrect: A v = 0v, so v is an eigenvector. Only the vector v itself must be nonzero.

misconceptions.feedback: Look at A v = 0 again. Can it be written as a number times v?

questions.prompt: The first column of P is (1, 1) for A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$. What is the first diagonal entry of D?
hints: D's entry is the eigenvalue of that column.
Work out A v for v = (1, 1).
Compare A v with v.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: This column has eigenvalue 3, so D's first diagonal entry is 3.

questions.onCorrect: A(1, 1) = 3(1, 1), so the first diagonal entry of D is 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a coordinate of the eigenvector. D holds eigenvalues.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ and v = (1, 1), what scalar multiplies v in A²v?
hints: What is the eigenvalue of v?
Each application multiplies v by it.
Multiply by the eigenvalue twice.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The eigenvalue is 3, so applying the map twice gives 3²v = 9v.

questions.onCorrect: Two applications multiply by 3 twice: 3² = 9.

misconceptions.feedback: That doubles the eigenvalue. Applying the map twice multiplies by it twice.
That is the eigenvalue itself, which covers one application.

questions.prompt: A 2 × 2 real matrix has only one independent real eigenvector direction. Can it be diagonalised over the reals?
hints: How many independent eigenvectors does P need?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. P needs two independent eigenvectors to be invertible.

questions.onCorrect: P needs a full set of independent eigenvectors. One direction is not enough in the plane.

misconceptions.feedback: P would need two independent eigenvector columns. With one direction it cannot be invertible.

questions.prompt: Now the first column of P is (1, −1) for A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$. What is the first diagonal entry of D?
hints: D's entry is the eigenvalue of that column.
Work out A v for this v.
Compare A v with v.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: This direction has eigenvalue 1, so the first diagonal entry must be 1.

questions.onCorrect: The eigenvalue travels with its eigenvector, so D's entries reorder with P's columns.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the eigenvalue for the other direction. Each eigenvalue stays beside its own vector.

questions.prompt: For A = $\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ and v = (1, 0), what scalar multiplies v in A³v?
hints: What is the eigenvalue of v?
Each application multiplies v by it.
Multiply by the eigenvalue three times.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The eigenvalue is 2, so three applications multiply by 2³ = 8.

questions.onCorrect: Three applications multiply by 2 three times: 2³ = 8.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the eigenvalue by three. Applying the map three times raises it to the third power.

questions.prompt: In A = P D P⁻¹, why must P be invertible?
hints: What does an invertible matrix say about its columns?

acceptedIdeas: Its columns must form a basis
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An invertible P has independent columns that span the space: a basis.

choices.label: Its columns must form a basis
Its columns must all be zero

questions.onCorrect: P is invertible exactly when its columns are a basis of eigenvectors.

misconceptions.feedback: Zero columns would make P collapse everything. P must be invertible.
The sign does not matter. It only has to be nonzero.

questions.prompt: What is the largest singular value of A = $\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&-2\end{pmatrix}$?
hints: The columns are perpendicular. How long is each?
Ignore the signs, because a flip is not a stretch.
Take the longer of the two lengths.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The two stretch magnitudes are 3 and 2, so the largest singular value is 3.

questions.onCorrect: The stretch sizes are 3 and 2. The sign of the second is just a flip.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the smaller stretch. The question asks for the largest.

questions.prompt: For a 2 × 3 matrix A, what is the shape of Σ in the full SVD?
hints: Σ must map the same inputs to the same outputs as A.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Σ has the same shape as A: 2 × 3.

questions.onCorrect: Σ takes the same inputs to the same outputs, so it has A's shape.

misconceptions.feedback: That would drop an input. Σ takes the same three inputs as A to the same two outputs.
That would add an output. Σ has the same shape as A.

questions.prompt: What is the smaller singular value of A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$?
hints: What is the rank of A?
The number of positive singular values equals the rank.
How many singular values does a two-by-two matrix have?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The matrix has rank one, so its second singular value is zero.

questions.onCorrect: Rank one means one positive singular value. The other is zero: the map flattens the plane to a line.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the larger singular value. The question asks for the smaller one.

questions.prompt: Which SVD factor performs the nonnegative stretching?
hints: Which factor is diagonal?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Σ holds the singular values. U and Vᵀ only turn.

questions.onCorrect: Σ is the diagonal stretch. U and Vᵀ preserve length.

misconceptions.feedback: U is orthogonal, so it only rotates or reflects.
Vᵀ is orthogonal, so it only rotates or reflects.

questions.prompt: What is the largest singular value of A = $\begin{pmatrix}0&5\\2&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$?
hints: The two columns are perpendicular. How long is each?
Ignore the zero row.
Take the longer of the two lengths.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The column directions are perpendicular with lengths 2 and 5; the largest stretch is 5.

questions.onCorrect: The columns are perpendicular, with lengths 2 and 5. The longest is the largest singular value.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the smaller stretch. The question asks for the largest.
That adds the two lengths. A stretch is measured along one direction.

questions.prompt: What is the smaller singular value of A = $\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&2&0\end{pmatrix}$?
hints: Which entries are the nonzero stretches?
Each row stretches along its own axis.
Take the smaller of the two stretches.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The two nonzero stretch factors are 2 and 1; the smaller is 1.

questions.onCorrect: The two nonzero stretches are 2 and 1, so the smaller singular value is 1.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the larger singular value. The question asks for the smaller one.

questions.prompt: How many blocks north of where you started are you now?
hints: Which of the two walks went north?
Both did. Only the north parts count here.
Add the two north distances.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The north parts are 1 and 3, so 1 + 3 = 4.

questions.onCorrect: 4. Across and up are tracked separately. Adding vectors adds each direction on its own.

misconceptions.feedback: That is only the second walk. The first one went north too.

hints: Add across to across, then up to up.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: (7, 8): 5 + 2 across and 1 + 7 up.

questions.onCorrect: Each coordinate adds to the one in the same position: across with across, up with up.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds across to up. Each coordinate adds only to the one in the same position.
That multiplies the first coordinates. Adding vectors only adds.

questions.prompt: Why do we multiply both coordinates of (3, −1) by 2?
hints: Picture the arrow getting twice as long.

acceptedIdeas: Scaling stretches the whole vector, so every coordinate grows by the same factor.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Stretching the whole arrow stretches both its across and up parts.

choices.label: Scaling stretches the whole vector, so every coordinate grows by the same factor.
Only the first coordinate changes when we scale.
The second coordinate must stay the same.

questions.onCorrect: A scalar stretches the whole arrow, so it multiplies every coordinate.

misconceptions.feedback: Then the arrow would change direction. Scaling keeps the direction, so both parts grow together.
Then the arrow would change direction. Both parts must grow by the same factor.

questions.prompt: What is the x coordinate of 3(−1, 2) + (4, −5)?
hints: Scale the first vector before adding.
Multiply both entries of the first vector by the scalar, then add matching entries.
The first entry of the scaled vector is negative. Add the other vector's first entry to it.
questions.onCorrect: Scale first: 3 × (−1) = −3. Then add the matching entry, 4.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts the second vector's entry instead of adding it.
That is the scaled entry alone. Add the other vector's entry.

questions.prompt: How many of the three moves can the robot lose and still reach every point?
hints: Is any of the three moves a combination of the other two?
Diagonal is right plus up.
Cross out that move. Can the other two still reach everywhere?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Diagonal is right plus up, so it can be dropped. Right and up alone still reach every point.

questions.onCorrect: A single redundant move can go. What remains, with no redundancy, is a basis.

misconceptions.feedback: With only a single move left, the robot could reach just a line. Try losing fewer.

questions.prompt: How many vectors are in a basis for ordinary three-dimensional space?
hints: Every basis has as many vectors as the space has dimensions.
How many dimensions does ordinary space have?
Count the independent directions: across, up and one more.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ordinary space has three dimensions, so every basis has three vectors.

questions.onCorrect: A basis has as many vectors as the space has dimensions.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the size of a basis for a plane. Ordinary space has a further direction.

questions.prompt: Why does a basis give each vector exactly one set of coordinates?
hints: There are two properties of a basis. Which gives existence, and which gives uniqueness?

acceptedIdeas: It spans, so every vector can be built, and it is independent, so there is only one way.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Spanning gives at least one way and independence gives at most one.

choices.label: It spans, so every vector can be built, and it is independent, so there is only one way.
Its vectors are always unit vectors.

questions.onCorrect: Spanning gives at least one way to build a vector. Independence allows at most one.

misconceptions.feedback: Basis vectors need not have length one. Spanning and independence do the work.
A basis can never contain the zero vector: it would be redundant.

questions.prompt: Write (8, 2) = c₁(1, 1) + c₂(1, −1). What is c₂?
hints: Match the first coordinates, then the second.
You get two equations in c₁ and c₂.
Subtract the second equation from the first so that c₁ cancels.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The equations are c₁ + c₂ = 8 and c₁ − c₂ = 2. Subtracting gives 2c₂ = 6, so c₂ = 3.

questions.onCorrect: Subtract the equations so c₁ cancels, then solve for c₂.

misconceptions.feedback: That is c₁. The question asks for c₂.

questions.prompt: How far up is the part that remains?
hints: Which part of the vector lies along the x axis?
Cutting it off leaves only the up part.
Read the up coordinate.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Removing the across part leaves (0, 7), which is 7 up.

questions.onCorrect: 7. Subtracting a vector's part along a direction leaves the part perpendicular to it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the across part, which has been removed.

questions.prompt: Subtract the projection of (2, 3) onto e₁ = (1, 0). What is the y coordinate of the residual?
hints: The projection onto (1, 0) keeps the across part.
Subtract it from the vector.
Only the up part is left.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The projection is (2, 0), so the residual is (0, 3).

questions.onCorrect: The residual is (0, 3): the part perpendicular to e₁.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the x coordinate of the residual. The question asks for y.

questions.prompt: Why must we normalise the residual after subtracting?
hints: Which property does subtracting give, and which does it not?

acceptedIdeas: Subtracting makes it perpendicular, but it need not have length 1.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Subtraction gives a right angle with the first vector. Only dividing by the length gives length one.

choices.label: Subtracting makes it perpendicular, but it need not have length 1.
Subtracting makes it longer than before.
Subtracting makes it parallel to the first vector.

questions.onCorrect: Subtracting gives a right angle, not unit length. Dividing by the length finishes the job.

misconceptions.feedback: Length is not the issue. The residual may be shorter or longer. It just is not fixed at one.
The opposite: subtracting the projection leaves a vector at a right angle to the first.

questions.prompt: Subtract the projection of (2, 4) onto (1, 1). What is the x coordinate of the residual?
hints: Find the coefficient (v · d) ÷ (d · d).
Scale d by it to get the projection.
Subtract the projection's x from v's x.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The coefficient is 6 ÷ 2 = 3, so the projection is (3, 3) and the residual is (−1, 1).

questions.onCorrect: The projection is (3, 3). Subtracting leaves (−1, 1), perpendicular to (1, 1).

misconceptions.feedback: The sign is missing. Subtract the projection's x from v's x, in that order.
That is the projection's x coordinate. The residual is what is left.

questions.prompt: How much bigger is the final number of the second run than the first?
hints: Work out each run in full.
In the first run, double 5 and then add. In the second, add and then double.
